The covenant itself — taken as a bride takes her husband's: to be called by His name is to be brought under His wing, whose corners carry the reminder of the commandments.

SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/01-introduction.adoc — opening

Shortly after feeding the five thousand, Jesus gave a hard teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum (John 6:59): “Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you… He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, dwelleth in me, and I in him” (John 6:53, 56).
After He said this, many of His disciples murmured — “This is an hard saying; who can hear it?” — and “from that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him” (John 6:60, 66).
It was so bad that Jesus turned to the twelve and asked whether they would also go away.

It was a hard saying because those who heard it did not know the symbolic language of the scriptures, and took it over-literally, saying: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” (John 6:52).
Which prompts the question: why would Jesus speak in a manner that drives people away?
Why not speak plainly?

He did it to fulfill the Scriptures, which prophesied that He would speak in parables.
When he spoke publicly he always used parables — “without a parable spake he not unto them” (Matthew 13:34) — and only with his closest disciples did he explain their meaning.
Even so, when he gave the parables of the kingdom his own disciples did not understand, and Jesus rebuked them for it. The rebuke was fair because the keys were already in the Old Testament: the “dark sayings of old” the psalm said he would utter (Mark 4:13; Psalm 78:2-3; Matthew 13:35). That exam waits a chapter ahead: The Parables of the Kingdom. [Footnote: The Parables of the Kingdom chapter derives each parable of Matthew 13 from the Old Testament alone.]

In other words, scripture prophesied that the message would be encrypted in parables and decoded with the Old Testament.
If you think you can read the New Testament without an intimate understanding of the Old, chances are you will walk away like the masses — either by interpreting it in a way you reject, or by misinterpreting it in a way you can accept, and facing the same consequences either way.

The first hearers of the apostles knew better.
When Paul preached in Berea, Luke recorded how the hearers received him — and graded them for it:

These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.

They tested Paul against the Old Testament, and Scripture calls that nobility.
How many today search the Old Testament to see whether their understanding of Paul is true?
The order has quietly reversed: Paul, as we understand him, has become the judge of the very scriptures he was judged by.
And the test is not for Paul only — your understanding of any verse must be tested against every other verse, for “at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established” (Deuteronomy 19:15): one verse cannot make a doctrine.

The Bible provides two symbolic words, meat and milk, to describe its teachings, and if you do not do the work to churn the milk into meat, you will remain immature at best — and at worst turn away entirely, like the crowds in Jesus’ day.

The purpose of this book is to teach you how I learned to chew the word of God and test everything.
It is a repeatable, reproducible process that has yielded more pearls of wisdom — and more appreciation for the supernatural structure of the word of God — than I could possibly fit in one book.
We will go through the process systematically and apply it to dozens of symbolic words, starting with meat and milk.
But first we must prepare the ground by explaining the difference between a word and a symbol.

===== NEXT SOURCE EXCERPT =====

SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/02-the-parables-of-the-kingdom.adoc — opening through How the Exam Is Taken

At the end of the seven parables of the kingdom, Jesus gave His hearers an exam of one question, and they passed it: “Yea, Lord.”
It had not started that way.
At the first parable — the key to all of them — His own disciples stumbled, and He rebuked them: “Know ye not this parable? and how then will ye know all parables?” (Mark 4:13).

Stop and weigh that rebuke.
A teacher may not be astonished that students fail an exam on material they were never given; His astonishment is only just if the answers were already on the table.
They were, and He said where.

The psalm He fulfills by teaching in parables locates the material in the past, not the future: “I will open my mouth in a parable: I will utter dark sayings of old: which we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us” (Psalm 78:2-3; Matthew 13:35).
And the Scriptures the disciples grew up on do not merely contain parables — they decode them in front of the reader and expect him to grade himself.

Nathan told David a story about a ewe lamb; David judged its villain to death without seeing his own face — “the man that hath done this thing shall surely die” (2 Samuel 12:5) — and Nathan handed him the key in four words: “Thou art the man” (2 Samuel 12:7).
Isaiah sang a parable of a vineyard, then handed over the key: “the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5:7).
Ezekiel told a riddle of two eagles and a vine, and God's next word is the very question Jesus would ask on the boat: “Know ye not what these things mean?” — followed by the answer, “the king of Babylon is come to Jerusalem” (Ezekiel 17:2, 12).

The exam is closed-book in one direction only: everything needed sits in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms.
Take each parable, then, the way a disciple on the shore had to take it — derive the meaning from the Scriptures he already had, write it down, and only then let the Teacher grade the work.
That is how this chapter will read them, and it will keep score.
More broadly, it will establish the principle of how to decode all of Scripture using the full body of the word.

Before the first parable, fix the procedure, because it is this book's whole method in miniature.
Take the parable's own words — sower, seed, ground, thorns, fowls — and search the Scriptures for the same words and phrases, everywhere they fall.
Where Scripture has already defined a term out loud — Isaiah's own key, above: the vineyard is the house of Israel — that definition is not local color for one passage; it holds, and it holds uniformly, or parables could not be decoded at all.

Next, weigh what you gathered before you lean on it.
One verse makes a candidate, not a key: a symbol is established when the pattern spans Moses and the prophets and the psalms — independent witnesses carrying the same figure, with no counter-text standing against them.
That standard is what makes the rebuke in the boat just, and it measures its weight: Jesus did not upbraid the twelve for missing an obscurity; seed and ground and thorns and fowls were established patterns, laid down across the whole of the Scriptures read to them every sabbath since childhood.
The better attested the pattern, the more accountable the hearer.

The difference between their seat and yours matters.
The disciple on the shore had his memory and the weekly reading; you have the whole text searchable in moments — a concordance, a search bar, and tools that can gather every use of a word while you frame your next question.
Recall was never the point of the exam, and now it is not even the obstacle: the test is not whether you remember the matches, but whether you go look for them.

===== NEXT SOURCE EXCERPT =====

SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/02-the-parables-of-the-kingdom.adoc — The Sower, Derived and Graded

“Behold, a sower went forth to sow” (Matthew 13:3).
Close the Gospels; what could a hearer of Moses and the prophets make of that?
Start with the seed, which Isaiah had defined in one breath with the rain:

For as the rain cometh down… that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater: so shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth…

The word is the seed to the sower and the bread to the eater — one verse, both figures.
And Moses had sung the same rain long before: “My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew” (Deuteronomy 32:2) — what falls from heaven to make the ground bear is teaching.

Next the ground.
Jeremiah had already preached this parable as a command: “Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns” — and his very next sentence names the soil: “take away the foreskins of your heart” (Jeremiah 4:3-4) — plowing and circumcising, one operation in two figures: remove the blocking flesh so the seed can enter.
Hosea gives the same order in the same words: “break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the LORD” (Hosea 10:12).
The ground is the heart, and the thorns were choking Judah's heart seven centuries before the sermon by the sea — and the thorns have a pedigree older still, for they are the curse-ground's own crop: “thorns also and thistles shall it (the ground) bring forth to thee” (Genesis 3:18), what the cursed earth grows where food should stand.

Now derive what the thorns mean, for the Old Testament assigns that too.
Read the sentence they grow in: the same curse that gives the ground its thorns sentences the man to anxious toil for his bread — “in sorrow shalt thou eat of it… in the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread” (Genesis 3:17, 19) — the thorns spring up in the field of the struggle for a living.
And that pair of weeds — thorn and thistle together — returns exactly once more in the Hebrew Scriptures, and Hosea builds the whole indictment around it:

Israel is an empty vine, he bringeth forth fruit unto himself: according to the multitude of his fruit he hath increased the altars; according to the goodness of his land they have made goodly images.
Their heart is divided; now shall they be found faulty…

The high places also of Aven, the sin of Israel, shall be destroyed: the thorn and the thistle shall come up on their altars; and they shall say to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us.

Increase, a divided heart, and the curse-ground's own crop sprouting on the altars: riches choking the heart is Hosea's picture before it is the parable's.

Isaiah's vineyard tells the same story, and he graded it himself.
The vineyard planted with the choicest vine gave wild grapes instead, and the sentence fell:

And I will lay it waste: it shall not be pruned, nor digged; but there shall come up briers and thorns: I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it.

Isaiah then hands over the key:

For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for judgment, but behold oppression; for righteousness, but behold a cry.

The vineyard is Israel, and its briers and thorns are men — the woes that follow name them, person by person:

Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth!

Here is the monopoly-builder — buying house after house and field after field until no one else has a place, alone in the middle of everything he has swallowed.

Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; that continue until night, till wine inflame them!
And the harp, and the viol, the tabret, and pipe, and wine, are in their feasts: but they regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands.

Here is the pleasure-lover — feasting from morning drink to evening music, past all notice of God.
Riches and pleasures came up where fruit should have stood: Isaiah graded the thorns seven centuries before the sermon by the sea.

Even the stony ground was on record, for the heart God promises to replace is “the stony heart” (Ezekiel 36:26).
And why is the exchange a heart of flesh for a heart of stone?
Because flesh is ground: adam was formed “of the dust of the ground,” adamah (Genesis 2:7) — the man is named for the soil he is — and he was sent forth “to till the ground from whence he was taken” (Genesis 3:23), so the Sower's field was staked out in Eden.
No one plows rock — “will one plow there with oxen?” (Amos 6:12) — and the very oracle that promises the heart of flesh promises its plowing: “I am for you… and ye shall be tilled and sown” (Ezekiel 36:9).
The seed that found “no deepness of earth” on stone takes root in flesh: the law once carved on “tables of stone” written now “in fleshy tables of the heart” (2 Corinthians 3:3) — “ye are God's husbandry” (1 Corinthians 3:9).

What does ground bring forth when the seed takes?
Grass — “all flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40:6) — a symbol with a chapter of its own.

What of the fowls that devour the wayside seed?
The first time birds descend on a covenant in Scripture, they come as devourers: “when the fowls came down upon the carcases, Abram drove them away” (Genesis 15:11) — uninvited, snatching at the covenant sacrifice, driven off by the covenant man.
In Egypt, Joseph heard a dream of birds eating baked bread out of a basket and graded it without hesitation as a sentence of death (Genesis 40:17-19).
Birds that snatch what was given out of its place are the enemy's agents; a boy raised on Genesis could have written that down.

.The Teacher grades the derivation

|===
| Element | Derived from the Law and the Prophets | The Teacher's key

| Seed
| The word — rain-borne seed, rain-borne doctrine (Isa 55:10-11; Deut 32:2)
| “The seed is the word of God” (Luke 8:11)

| Ground
| The heart — plowed, circumcised, tilled and sown (Jer 4:3-4; Hos 10:12; Ezek 36:9, 26; Gen 2:7)
| The word “sown in his heart” (Matt 13:19)

| Fowls
| The devourers on the covenant and on the bread (Gen 15:11; 40:17-19)
| “Then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown” (Matt 13:19)

| Thorns
| The curse-crop; riches dividing the heart (Gen 3:17-19; Hos 10:1-8; Isa 5:6-12)
| “The care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word” (Matt 13:22)
|===

Four for four — Isaiah's answer, Jeremiah's, Abram's, Hosea's — and not one of the four needed a word Jesus had not yet spoken.
His astonishment in Mark 4:13 was just.

Yet let me be fair, for I would have fared no better.
Handed the parable with no Bible in reach, I would have failed it as completely as any man on the shore.
With a Bible and a printed concordance — and the assurance that the answer was in there somewhere — the derivation above might have cost me days, or months.
It is only with modern tools that I can derive the interpretation independently at all, without leaning on any man's commentary.

Daniel was told to seal the words “even to the time of the end,” when “many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased” (Daniel 12:4).
The running to and fro is through the scriptures themselves — and the knowledge increased is this.

SOURCE: books/symbolic-language/08-the-name.adoc

Two things almost everyone believes about “the name” turn out to be wrong, and they are the two doors most people walk in by.
The first: that to “take the LORD’s name in vain” is to curse — “oh my God” as an idle breath — or to mangle the sacred syllables, YHWH, Yahweh, Yahuah.
The second is quieter.
We end our prayers “in Jesus’ name,” as though the phrase were a key that turns the lock — and when nothing turns, we quietly wonder what went wrong.

Both mistakes treat the name as a sound: a word to pronounce correctly, or a formula to attach.
But Jesus made a promise about His name that no magic word could keep:

And whatsoever ye shall ask in my name, that will I do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son.

Whatsoever — and yet how many prayers, sealed with the name, go unanswered?
Either the promise fails, or “in my name” means something deeper than a phrase we append.
To find it we must stop asking how the name sounds and ask what it is — and Scripture builds the answer a piece at a time.

Begin with that promise.
To ask “in my name” is not to invoke a syllable but to ask as one who belongs to Him — within His will, on His terms, inside the relationship.
Paul says the same of the whole of life: “whatsoever ye do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus” (Colossians 3:17).
You cannot do everything by pronouncing a word over it; you can only do everything within a relationship.
To act “in the name” is to act inside the bond.

The bond is something a person carries.
At Sinai, God named the guide who went before His people — one with the name itself in him:

Behold, I send an Angel before thee, to keep thee in the way, and to bring thee into the place which I have prepared… Beware of him, and obey his voice, provoke him not; for he will not pardon your transgressions: for my name is in him.

This is no created messenger.
He bears God’s own name — His presence and authority — and Scripture, looking back, tells us plainly who he was: “the angel of his presence saved them… and he bare them, and carried them all the days of old” (Isaiah 63:9).
The Rock that followed Israel through the wilderness, Paul says, “was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4).
So Christ — the One in whom the name dwelt — led them by the pillar of cloud and fire; and the same One came in the flesh.
(One clause does reach ahead: this Angel “will not pardon your transgressions” — and transgress they did, at the very foot of the mountain; the name-bearer who would at last pardon comes only when He takes flesh.)

When Jesus says “I have declared unto them thy name” (John 17:26), He is not reciting a sound He learned; He is that name-bearer, now walking among His people — the name borne in a person, made visible in a faithful life, and kept the way it always was: He keeps them “in the way” (covenant-conduct); they must “obey his voice.”

The promise looked beyond that generation’s journey.
The Angel was sent “to bring thee into the place which I have prepared” — the very words the name-bearer would take up as His own: “I go to prepare a place for you… I will come again, and receive you unto myself” (John 14:2-3).
The One in whom the name dwells led Israel through the wilderness, came in the flesh, and will come again to gather His people into the place He has prepared — one name-bearer, from the wilderness to the end.

Which sets up the sharpest test Jesus ever gave.
Picture the people most certain of their standing:

Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many powers? [Footnote: The King James prints “wonderful works”; the Greek is dynameis — powers, not erga, works.]
And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work lawlessness.

Every sentence has the name in it — prophesying, casting out devils, doing powers “in thy name.”
No one ever spoke it more.
He turns them away as “workers of lawlessness” — anomia.
They had the sound and not the substance.

The name cannot be a word on the lips: a man may have it there constantly and remain a stranger to the One who bears it.
What, then, is it?

Here at last Scripture says it outright.
David, settled in his palace, wants to build a house for the ark of the covenant:

…I dwell in an house of cedar, but the ark of God dwelleth within curtains.

God answers, and quietly trades one word for another:

He shall build an house for my name, and I will stablish the throne of his kingdom for ever.

David said the ark of the covenant; God said my name.
They are the same thing.
The name is the covenant [Footnote: Covenant — the renewed covenant of the kingdom; see the Gospel chapter.] — the binding relationship between God and His people.

Notice that God, answering, plays on David’s own word — for a “house” in Scripture is a building and a family line, and a family line is exactly what carries a name.
David offered to build God a house of stone; God replies, “the LORD telleth thee that he will make thee an house” (2 Samuel 7:11) — not cedar but sons: the house of David.

The promise then stands established three ways at once, and every level holds.
In the flesh: the seed and throne endure — “the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David… and of his kingdom there shall be no end” (Luke 1:32-33).
In stone: Solomon raises the temple “for my name.”
And in covenant: the Son of David builds the house the first two only sketched — “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up… he spake of the temple of his body” (John 2:19-21); “ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house” (1 Peter 2:5); “Christ as a son over his own house; whose house are we” (Hebrews 3:6).

Zechariah compresses the whole promise into one oracle:

…Behold the man whose name is The BRANCH; and he shall grow up out of his place, and he shall build the temple of the LORD:
Even he shall build the temple of the LORD; and he shall bear the glory, and shall sit and rule upon his throne; and he shall be a priest upon his throne: and the counsel of peace shall be between them both.

Name, house, and throne in one Man.
The wordplay is the doctrine: a house exists to carry a name, and God’s answer to David binds His name and David’s house into a single building.

Now everything before falls into place: this is why asking “in his name” is asking within the covenant; why the name is borne by the obedient; why the man who only speaks it is unknown.
And it is why “there is none other name under heaven… whereby we must be saved” (Acts 4:12): no other name, because no other covenant.
To “believe on his name” (John 1:12) is not to credit a title but to enter that covenant in trusting obedience.

It is also why the name can be a refuge:

The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe.

No one takes shelter inside a sound.
A covenant can be run into — walls, a roof, and a door that shuts behind the one who keeps it.

It even untangles an old puzzle.
God tells Moses He was “not known” to the patriarchs “by my name JEHOVAH” (Exodus 6:3) — though Abraham plainly heard the word, “I am the LORD that brought thee out of Ur” (Genesis 15:7).
He knew the sound; he had not yet entered the covenant that name would come to carry.

Which is exactly why the argument over the right syllables, earnest as it is, looks straight past the thing itself.
The name is not a sound to recover.
It is a covenant to keep.

Now — and only now — the commandment opens:

Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain.

“Vain” is shav — emptiness, for nothing.
To take the name in vain is to take the covenant for nothing: to wear it, claim it, swear by it, while living as though it asks nothing of you.
It was never first a sin of the mouth; it is a sin of the life.
The cursing man breaks it, yes — but so does the one who cries “Lord, Lord” and works lawlessness, and the one who seals empty prayers with a name he will not keep.

Solomon files that exact case:

He that turneth away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer shall be abomination.

The mouth full of the name, the ear turned from the covenant that fills it: such prayer does not merely go unanswered, it offends.
There is the answer to the puzzle this chapter opened with: the prayer sealed “in the name” fails because the ear has left the law.
Most who take His name in vain do it inside the church.

The prophets prosecute the same sin under another verb.
“When they entered unto the heathen… they profaned my holy name, when they said to them, These are the people of the LORD, and are gone forth out of his land” (Ezekiel 36:20).
Israel did not profane the name by mispronouncing it; they profaned it by wearing it faithlessly in front of the nations — covenant-breakers introduced everywhere as the covenant people.
And God’s remedy is not a correction of speech: “I will sanctify my great name, which was profaned among the heathen… when I shall be sanctified in you before their eyes” (Ezekiel 36:23) — He hallows His own name by making the people who wear it holy.

The most familiar prayer in the world asks for exactly this — and once the name is understood, the whole prayer opens, line by line.
Its grammar carries more weight than the recitation lets on.
“Hallowed be thy name” (Matthew 6:9) is not a description and not a compliment; the verb is an imperative: let thy name be made holy — the one praying is demanding the very thing Ezekiel promised, that the name be hallowed in its people before the eyes of the world.

Hear the petitions that march out behind it, each in the same commanding mood: “Thy kingdom come.
Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven” (Matthew 6:10).
Name hallowed, kingdom come, will done — the covenant kept holy in a people, the King’s reign arriving, and His will obeyed on earth the way heaven already obeys it.
The second petition tells us how the first is granted: a name is hallowed when the will of its Bearer is done — beginning with the one praying.

The covenant runs through every petition that follows; walk them with the Bible’s symbolic language in hand.
“Give us this day our daily bread” (Matthew 6:11) — and bread is a defined symbol: the word from the mouth of the LORD (Deuteronomy 8:3).
The petition even has a history, for the first daily bread was the manna — rained from heaven one day’s portion at a time, and God states His purpose in the giving: “that I may prove them, whether they will walk in my law, or no” (Exodus 16:4).

Luke’s wording keeps the manna’s rhythm exactly — “Give us day by day our daily bread” (Luke 11:3) — and when Luke’s Jesus finishes the prayer, He walks straight into a parable of a man begging three loaves at midnight and a Father who gives to them that ask (Luke 11:5-13): the petition, dramatized.
To ask for daily bread is to ask for the day’s portion of the word — and to take up the day’s test of walking in it.

“And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12).
The release of debts is the law’s own mercy — “every creditor that lendeth ought unto his neighbour shall release it… because it is called the LORD’S release” (Deuteronomy 15:2) — and the petition asks God to run His release toward us as we run it toward our brothers.
Luke’s version glosses the symbol as it goes: “And forgive us our sins; for we also forgive every one that is indebted to us” (Luke 11:4) — sins in the first clause, debtors in the second: the two gospels set the columns side by side, and the debt is sin.

It is the one line of the prayer Jesus stops to underline the moment He finishes teaching it — “For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you: but if ye forgive not…” (Matthew 6:14-15) — and He later stages it as a full drama: the servant forgiven ten thousand talents who takes his brother by the throat, and is delivered back to the tormentors (Matthew 18:32-35).
The prayer must be practiced by the man praying it, or it testifies against him.

The last petition asks the covenant God for the covenant deliverance: “lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matthew 6:13).
Both halves repay testing.

“Temptation” translates a Greek word that means the proving, and James rules out the modern reading in one stroke: “God cannot be tempted with evil, neither tempteth he any man” (James 1:13) — yet the same James calls the man blessed who endures it: “when he is tried, he shall receive the crown of life” (James 1:12).

Beneath the Greek stands a Hebrew word the King James renders both ways, and the wobble is our familiar signpost: “God did tempt Abraham” (Genesis 22:1) — the first “tempt” in the Bible, in the very scene that gives us the first “worship” (Genesis 22:5, a discovery the Worship chapter will unfold) — is the same word as “that I may prove them” over the manna (Exodus 16:4), and “to prove thee… whether thou wouldest keep his commandments, or no” (Deuteronomy 8:2); David even prays for it: “prove me” (Psalm 26:2).
The petition, then, does not imagine God dangling sin; it pleads about the furnace-hour of proving — “the hour of temptation, which shall come upon all the world, to try them” (Revelation 3:10) — the same plea Jesus pressed on His sleeping disciples in Gethsemane: “Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation” (Matthew 26:41).

The plea “deliver us from evil” is personal in the Greek — deliver us from the evil one: the same “wicked one” who snatches the sown word and fathers the tares (Matthew 13:19, 38).
Watch the Name-bearer pray this very petition over a man:

…Simon, Simon, behold, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat:
But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren.

Trial itself is not prayed away — the manna was given to prove — the plea is to be brought through the proving and out of the destroyer’s hand, with the promise standing behind it: God “will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape” (1 Corinthians 10:13).

Read whole, the prayer Jesus taught is the covenant renewed in miniature: the name hallowed, the kingdom summoned, the will obeyed, the word received daily, the release practiced, the deliverance promised.
Every line of it is prayed “in the name,” because every line of it lives inside the covenant — and its salvation is promised to those who practice what they pray.

How, then, is the name kept full rather than emptied?
By its terms — the law.
Moses binds the two in a single line:

If thou wilt not observe to do all the words of this law that are written in this book, that thou mayest fear this glorious and fearful name, THE LORD THY GOD…

Keep the law and you honor the name; despise the law and you empty it.
So at the very end of the story, the people who belong to God are marked by that exact pairing — “they that keep the commandments of God, and the faith of Jesus” (Revelation 14:12) — with “his Father’s name written in their foreheads” (Revelation 14:1): the covenant owned and worn where all can see — the seal set on God’s servants.
Scripture binds the name and the law together, and will not let them be pried apart.

In the Bible’s symbolic language, many symbols come paired with an opposite — and describing the opposite often sheds light on the meaning of its counterpart.
The name has such an opposite, and it is the oldest counterfeit on record.

On the plain of Shinar the builders said, “let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name” (Genesis 11:4) — Babel, the kingdom whose founding act is a self-made name: an identity manufactured from below, a covenant with no one above.
God’s answer stands in the very next chapter, spoken to one man called out of that world: “I will make of thee a great nation, and I will bless thee, and make thy name great” (Genesis 12:2).
A made name or a given one — the whole war of the Bible in two clauses.

The war ends on men’s foreheads.
The beast “causeth all… to receive a mark in their right hand, or in their foreheads… the name of the beast” (Revelation 13:16-17); one chapter later, the Lamb’s company stands on mount Sion “having his Father’s name written in their foreheads” (Revelation 14:1).
There is no unmarked forehead in that scene.
Everyone wears a name — the one men make for themselves, or the one God gives — and the commandment asks which one you will refuse to carry for nothing.

One question remains: how does a person come to bear a name that is not his own?
Scripture answers with the oldest institution it has — a bride takes her husband’s — and Isaiah shows the formula in a single desperate verse:

And in that day seven women shall take hold of one man, saying, We will eat our own bread, and wear our own apparel: only let us be called by thy name, to take away our reproach.

To be “called by thy name” is to be married — that is the whole request — and the women’s bargain proves it: the law obliges a husband to supply his wife’s “food, her raiment, and her duty of marriage” (Exodus 21:10), and these seven offer to waive everything but the name itself.
Read in the Bible’s symbolic language, the bargain turns chilling.

Seven women — seven, the number Scripture gives the assemblies of God’s people (Revelation 1:20) — asking to wear the Bridegroom’s name while eating their own bread and wearing their own apparel: their own word in place of His, their own righteousness in place of His.
It is the “Lord, Lord” of Matthew 7 spoken as a marriage proposal — the name, minus the covenant that fills it.
And the true Husband gives His widowed people exactly the two things these women decline — “food and raiment” (Deuteronomy 10:18): the bread of His word and the garment of His righteousness. [Footnote: The food and the raiment are opened fully in the Orphans, Widows, and the Fatherless chapter.]

The true marriage is enacted through the same covenant mechanics.
When Ruth asks Boaz for marriage, she asks him to spread the corner of his garment over her (Ruth 3:9) — and “skirt” there is the Hebrew kanaph, the wing: the covenant edge.

For Ruth is everything the seven women are not, and her story keeps the ledger.
She brings no bread of her own: she eats at Boaz’s table until she “was sufficed, and left” (Ruth 2:14), gleans his field by the law of the corner — with “handfuls of purpose” dropped in her path (Ruth 2:16) — and is sent home under six measures of barley with the charge, “Go not empty” (Ruth 3:17).
And the only raiment the story provides her is the one she asks for.
Boaz had blessed her, “a full reward be given thee of the LORD God of Israel, under whose wings thou art come to trust” (Ruth 2:12) — and on the threshing floor she asks him to make good his own blessing in person: the widow’s garment laid aside (Ruth 3:3), and one covering requested — his.

God describes His own wedding to Israel with the same gesture:

Now when I passed by thee, and looked upon thee, behold, thy time was the time of love; and I spread my skirt over thee, and covered thy nakedness: yea, I sware unto thee, and entered into a covenant with thee, saith the Lord GOD, and thou becamest mine.

There the raiment clause is written out in full, in the verses that follow the spread skirt: “Then washed I thee… I anointed thee… I clothed thee also with broidered work… and I covered thee with silk… thy raiment was of fine linen… thou didst eat fine flour, and honey, and oil” (Ezekiel 16:9-13) — food and raiment, both from the Husband, exactly the provision the seven women waived.

To take the husband’s name is to come under the husband’s wing — and the wing’s corners carry the tassels, bound there so that the wearer remembers all the commandments of the LORD and does them (Numbers 15:38-39).
The covering a bride enters when she takes the name is stitched at every corner with the reminder of the law of the One who spreads it — and a bleeding woman once took hold of that corner in faith, and the name did what no sound can (Matthew 9:20-21). [Footnote: The wing, the fringe bound at its corner, and the healing found there are derived in the Wings chapter.]
The name and the commandments arrive as one garment — which is why the name is kept by keeping the law (Deuteronomy 28:58), and emptied any other way.

This grasp is the gesture the nations finally learn.
Isaiah’s seven women “take hold” of one man; Zechariah sees the same verb close on the right thing:

…ten men shall take hold out of all languages of the nations, even shall take hold of the skirt of him that is a Jew, saying, We will go with you: for we have heard that God is with you.

The hand closes on the kanaph — the wing-corner where the commandments hang — and the words are Ruth’s own, the Moabite bride who said “whither thou goest, I will go” (Ruth 1:16).

Ruth’s wedding under the wing leads directly into this chapter’s closing point.
The law states the purpose of a kinsman’s marriage in name-language: the son is raised “that his name be not put out of Israel,” and the man who refuses is shamed as one who “will not build up his brother’s house” (Deuteronomy 25:6, 9) — in the law’s own grammar, building a house and raising a name are one act.
So Boaz declares he has taken Ruth “to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance” (Ruth 4:10); the elders bless her as one come to “build the house” (Ruth 4:11); and the house that wedding built was the house of David (Ruth 4:17) — the very house God would answer with a house for His own name.

A bride under the wing, a name raised, a house built — and in the fulness of time, a Son of that house who is Himself the temple.
The symbols do not merely repeat; they compound.

The symbol gathers up the ones before it.
The gospel is the covenant announced; the way, the truth, and the life are the covenant embodied; the name is the covenant owned — taken upon yourself as a bride takes her husband’s, to keep or to empty.
Most who cry “Lord, Lord” wear it for nothing.
To bear it in truth is to keep the covenant of the One in whom the name dwells — and so to be known by Him in that day.
And the name owned is also written — impressed on its bearers like a signet in wax.
Where God sets it, what it says, and what counterfeit stamps the same two places — that is the seal, and it is the Seal chapter.
